newsitem.title: USA: Airlines to appeal Miami AMR rate ruling.
newsitem.headline: Airlines to appeal Miami AMR rate ruling.

text.p: The six airlines that challenged the funding for American Airlines' new terminal at Miami International Airport will appeal a federal ruling that found the rate strucuture fair, the plaintiffs' attorney said.
Attorney Barry Davidson said Thursday the carriers "absolutely" would appeal to the Federal Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia within 30 days.
"This is hardly the end of the trail," Davidson told Reuters.
The U.S. Department of Transportation ruled Wednesday the airport's plan to require its 92 passenger airlines to share the cost of American's new $975 million terminal was fair and reasonable.
American, a unit of AMR Corp, said it was prepared to meet the appeal.
"We can't imagine on what basis they would appeal, since the DOT was quite emphatic on these issues," American spokesman Al Becker said.

The plaintiffs had sued Florida's Dade County, which runs the airport, saying their rates would unfairly be raised to pay for the terminal that will be used exclusively by American. The funding formula divides the cost among the carriers according to the number of flights they operate.
The plaintiffs are Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Trans World Airlines Inc, United Airlines, Lufthansa and US Airways Group Inc.

The DOT ruling ignored the recommendation of an administrative law judge, who said last month the fee-sharing plan was discriminatory because the new American terminal would be a "Taj Mahal" compared with the facilities the other carriers use.
American argued that the fee-sharing structure had long been used at Miami and other airports and said American often helped pay for facilities it does not use.

The American terminal is part of a $4 billion, 10-year expansion at the airport, which will add a fourth runway, expanded cargo space and a new terminal for the other carriers. American is the dominant carrier at the Miami airport, accounting for more than 50 percent of its flights.

Airport Director Gary Dellapa and Commissioner Natacha Millan, who chairs Dade County's aviation operations committee, released a joint statement praising the ruling and pledging to "work to gain the support of our major carriers."

Airport spokeswoman Lauren Gail said the ruling clears the way for the aviation department to issue $240 million of airport revenue bonds in November for the next phase of expansion. It was unclear what impact the appeal would have on the bond issue.

United's vice president for property and facilities, Larry Clark, called the DOT ruling "unfair and unwise" and said it set a dangerous precedent for other airports. He said the rate increases would be passed on to passengers.

"This is an unfortunate setback for competition in Dade County and for travelers across the country and around the world who use the Miami gateway," Clark said. "The current plan forces air carriers competing against American Airlines to pay for improvements that will only benefit American Airlines."

The plaintiffs filed their lawsuit last year in U.S. District Court in Miami. The trial judge, U.S. District Judge Joan Leonard, said she lacked jurisdiction to rule on the rate structure, which the DOT regulates.

Several remaining issues in the lawsuit are still pending before Leonard, including whether or not the major carriers' contract with the airport gives them the right to approve major expansion projects, Davidson said.
